name: Jade Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the depot on Mill Road by six, and the first thing I do is check the trucks before the boys get their coffee down. I lead a crew of four out of a small hill-country depot, so a day might be swapping a rotten pole on a farm road, fixing a sagging span after a tree came down, or chasing a fault nobody can find. I love it when the power comes back on and you see the porch lights go on all down the valley. What wears me out is the paperwork on that blasted tablet and my knees on the climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the tablet. How do you get on with the technology side of the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Badly, and I don't mind saying so. The company gave us tablets for work orders three years ago and I still get young Dev to fill mine in while I drink my tea. I've never used one of these AI chat things and I don't plan to. Thirty-four years I've done this with my hands and my eyes, and I can tell a bad insulator by the hum before any screen can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. I'll read each one out as written. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for years: told you so. At the depot we'd have a laugh about the head office people who spent a fortune on gadgets. Online I don't really post, but I'd share it in the union group chat that Tom set up for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I do until I'm 65, and that suits me. My worry was never really the robots. It's that I've got next to nothing put by and seven years to go, and that doesn't change whether the computers get clever or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep the overtime on storm call-outs because that's where the extra money is, and I'd keep pushing the company on the next pay deal. Maybe I'd finally sort out a proper savings account instead of the jar on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, I think. It feels like being told the storm went the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say the money's tight even if nothing changes, what does that look like week to week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Friday pay going straight out on the mortgage, the truck loan for Tom's car, and topping up Kirsty since her divorce. We pay less here than the city crews get, everybody knows it, and the rural allowance hasn't moved in years. If the washing machine went tomorrow it would go on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the union side of things. Would anything change there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the point. We'd still be fighting the same fight: the company keeps the crews thin and calls it efficiency. AI or no AI, I'll be sitting across that table next spring asking why a crew of four is covering a district that had six when I started.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone at the depot that I'd been saying it was hype all along. I'd share it in the union group chat and have a laugh about head office wasting money on gadgets.
S0.think: Privately, my real problem was never robots but having almost nothing saved with seven years to go. That stays the same whether computers get smarter or not.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and takes storm overtime for the extra money. Keeps pushing the company in pay talks and means to open a proper savings account instead of the jar on the fridge.
S0.feel: Relieved, like hearing a storm has turned away, though the money worry stays in the background.
S0.quote: The rural allowance hasn't moved in years. If the washing machine went tomorrow it would go on the card.
S0.fieldNote: Jade sees the AI question through the lens of crew sizes and pay, not technology. Her calm here is about the job staying the same; the thin savings are a separate worry she lives with already. She proudly avoids the tablet and lets an apprentice do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union in the room from day one, not after the fact. With friends I'd say it's the same old story: the company gets a new toy and the crew gets smaller. I'd want rules written down about what a machine can and can't do on a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, probably. I'm senior, I'm good, and nobody's sending a robot up a pole in a gale on a farm track in the next few years. But I'd have to learn new gear and I'm slow with that, and I hate the idea of some young manager timing me against a drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name forward for the union committee on new technology, because I'd rather fight it from inside. I'd keep working the same, keep the overtime and try to get fifty or so a week into savings, though I'll be honest, that never lasts. I wouldn't go on any course unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the truck you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tablet already took a man off the crew in your eyes. Can you tell me more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the tablets came, they stopped sending a dispatcher out with us on big jobs because the screen does the routing now. That was Pete's job, and Pete took early retirement on a pittance. So when people tell me AI just helps you, I think of Pete at the garden centre stacking compost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my apprentice. He's 22, he's good with screens, but he hasn't got the feel for the line yet. If they cut training years because a machine does half the job, he never gets the feel, and then who looks after the valley when I'm gone?

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be in the room from day one, with written rules on what machines can do on a live line. To friends I'd call it the same old story of new toys and smaller crews.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd probably be fine because I'm senior and good, and robots won't climb poles in gales soon. But learning new gear is hard for me and I'd hate being timed against a drone.
S1.do: Joins the union committee on new technology to fight changes from inside. Keeps working and taking overtime, and tries to save about fifty a week, though she admits it rarely lasts.
S1.feel: A low unease, like a noise in the truck she can't place yet.
S1.quote: When people tell me AI just helps you, I think of Pete at the garden centre stacking compost.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear of change is grounded in a real memory: a dispatcher lost his role when tablets came in. She places her hope in the union, not in learning anything new. Her worry quickly shifts to her apprentice rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster pictures. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, I think, for once. I'd say the government has to stop it or pay people properly while it happens, because you can't just switch off a whole workforce. At the depot I'd be organising meetings in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'm out before my pension. Two years, I'd be 60, and if the company can put a robot on the line cheaper, they'll do it, and they'll start with the expensive old hands like me. There's no other line company within an hour's drive, and nobody's hiring a 60-year-old woman to do anything else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food, mortgage and fuel, starting that week. I'd push the union to demand proper payouts and a bridge to the pension, and I'd go to every meeting and march. I'm not going to retrain at 59 in two years for a job a machine will do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor going out from under you while you're still on the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is the last thing to go, so it'd be the card first, then Tom's car loan. We'd stop helping Kirsty, which would break my heart. We've maybe three weeks of money if I'm honest, so it wouldn't take long to be in real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kirsty and Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum's going to be fine, which would be a lie. Ben would want to send money and I'd refuse. Then I'd sit in the truck in the driveway for a bit before going in, the way I did when my dad died.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that the government has to stop it or pay people properly while it happens. At the depot I'd be organising meetings in the canteen.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd be pushed out at 60, before my pension, with the expensive old hands going first. There's no other line company within an hour and nobody would hire me for anything else.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food, mortgage and fuel straight away. Pushes the union for payouts and a bridge to her pension, attends every meeting and march, and refuses to retrain for a job she expects to be automated too.
S2.feel: Sick and shaken, like the floor going out from under her while she's still on the ladder.
S2.quote: I'd tell them Mum's going to be fine, which would be a lie.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her thin savings show. She has about three weeks of money and no local alternative, and she knows it. Her answer is collective: the union, marches and government, never a personal pivot. The image of sitting in the truck in the driveway was very quiet and very real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing as the fast one, but I'd say it with more fight in it. We'd have time to get laws passed, so I'd be telling everyone to vote for whoever promises to protect workers and tax the companies that use robots. I'd say it at work and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad but it's not the cliff edge. Five years gets me to 63, and that's close enough that maybe a deal could carry me the last two years. The question is whether the union can win that deal in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting real money by now, even if it's only forty a week, and I'd cut the cable TV and the takeaways. I'd go hard on the union side, pushing for an early retirement deal for over-55s. And I'd help Tom look for steadier hours on the buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That's better than just being scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you at 63. Does that change the maths on your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. If I could go at 63 with a reduced pension and a lump from a deal, we'd scrape by, provided we're done with the mortgage. That's a big if, because we've got eight years left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you wouldn't go on a course unless they made you. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I know that sounds stubborn. But I'd sooner spend five years fighting for a decent exit than learning a machine that's coming for whatever I learn next.

S3.say: I'd tell people at work and at the pub to vote for whoever promises to protect workers and tax companies that use robots. I'd say there's time to get laws passed.
S3.think: Privately it's still bad but not a cliff edge, since five years gets me to 63. A deal might carry me the last two years, if the union wins it in time.
S3.do: Starts saving around forty a week and cuts cable TV and takeaways. Pushes the union for an early retirement deal for over-55s and helps her partner look for steadier hours.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, because there's something she can do about it.
S3.quote: I'd sooner spend five years fighting for a decent exit than learning a machine that's coming for whatever I learn next.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shift her from alarm to planning, but the plan is all about a fair exit, not adapting. She names her own stubbornness openly. The mortgage's eight remaining years is the number that decides everything for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be gone by then, so it's the young ones I'm worried for. At union meetings I'd be pushing for apprentices to be kept on and paid while they learn whatever comes next. That's what I'd say to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I probably get out the door just in time. I'd be 68 in 2036 and I plan to stop at 65. It's a strange thing to feel lucky about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and work my last years out. I'd still try to put a bit aside each month, maybe thirty, because a decade of warning is no use if you've got nothing at the end. And I'd fight for Dev and the others through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the young ones, mostly. For me it's closer to relief, and I feel a bit guilty saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this one, would anything in your life actually change in the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to be truthful. I'd keep the overtime, nag the company about the next pay deal, and try to stick to the savings. The big change would be in how I talk to Dev about his future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the valley itself? The people you keep the lights on for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd miss. When a storm takes out the line to old Mrs Carver's farm, she rings me, not the call centre. A robot might fix the line, but it won't know she's on oxygen and needs to be first.

S4.say: I'd say I'll be gone by then so it's the young ones I worry for. At union meetings I'd push for apprentices to be kept on and paid while they learn whatever comes next.
S4.think: Privately it means I probably get out just in time, retiring at 65 before it lands at 68. It's a strange thing to feel lucky about.
S4.do: Keeps working her last years as normal and tries to save around thirty a month. Fights through the union for her apprentice and other young workers to be kept on and trained.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the young workers and quietly relieved for herself, with some guilt about that relief.
S4.quote: A robot might fix the line, but it won't know she's on oxygen and needs to be first.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her own risk mostly drops away because her retirement comes first. Her concern moves outward to her apprentice and the people on her lines. She still won't plan a pivot, but she doesn't need one here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd be out at 60 with three weeks of money and no other line company within an hour. What would help is a proper bridge to my pension, paid by the companies that bring in the robots, and the union having a legal right to be at the table when they do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who keeps the robots honest. When something goes wrong on a live line, somebody has to stand there and say no, that's not safe. I've said it a hundred times in thirty-four years, and I'd want to know who says it after me.

headlineQuote: When something goes wrong on a live line, somebody has to stand there and say no, that's not safe.
portrait: Jade Olsen is a 58-year-old crew leader at a small hill-country depot, a union stalwart who has done the job with her hands for 34 years and lets her apprentice fill in her tablet. She has about three weeks of money saved, lower pay than city crews, and no other line company within an hour's drive. A plateau or slow change barely moves her, because she sees AI as one more excuse for thinner crews and trusts the union to fight it. Fast AGI in two years alarms her, because she'd be pushed out at 60 before her pension. With five or ten years she moves towards planning a fair exit, and her worry turns to her apprentice and the people on her lines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be out at 60 with about three weeks of money and no other line work nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to her pension paid for by the companies bringing in robots, and a legal right for the union to be at the table when they do.
